content: 1. No method failures were documented in either group during the 6-month follow-up period. However, the effect of pharmacist-administered injectable contraception on method failure at 6 months remains unknown due to the absence of reported events. The certainty of this evidence is very low. 2. All three pharmacists involved in administering subcutaneous depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA-SC) injections expressed a high level of comfort with their clinical role. They felt either somewhat or very informed about DMPA-SC and were comfortable or somewhat comfortable administering urine pregnancy tests when applicable. They were very comfortable checking blood pressures and administering the injections. All three pharmacists expressed a desire to continue offering DMPA-SC injections in their pharmacy practice. 3. All five Planned Parenthood providers had a positive overall perception of the clinical arrangement with the pharmacy. They were either somewhat or very comfortable knowing their patients were receiving DMPA-SC injections from a clinical pharmacist. One provider felt it was very appropriate for pharmacists to administer DMPA-SC, three felt it was somewhat appropriate, and one remained neutral. 4. Evidence suggests that pharmacist-administered injectable contraception may have little to no effect on healthcare provider satisfaction at 6 months. Both groups reported high satisfaction levels, but the evidence is very uncertain. 5. The risk of method failure with DMPA-SC administered by usual family planning providers versus pharmacists could not be determined due to the lack of reported events and the very low certainty of evidence. 6. Evidence from observational studies suggests that telemedicine for medical abortion care results in little to no difference in complete abortion rates, ongoing pregnancies, or satisfaction compared to in-person care. However, the certainty of this evidence is very low. 7. Telemedicine may result in a small reduction in the need for surgical abortion referrals, but the certainty of this evidence is also very low. 8. There is little to no difference in contraception uptake following abortion when comparing telemedicine to in-person care, but the certainty of this evidence remains very low. 9. No hospitalizations or deaths were reported in either group during follow-up periods of up to 2 or 4 months, respectively. However, the certainty of this evidence is very low. 10. Evidence suggests that telemedicine may result in little to no difference in overall satisfaction or the likelihood of participants recommending the service to a friend. However, the certainty of this evidence is very low. 11. The evidence base for telemedicine in medical abortion care is limited by critical risks of bias, including non-randomized study designs, confounding factors, and selection bias. Additionally, sample sizes were small, and no adjustments for confounders were made in the analyzed studies. 12. The choice of service delivery models for abortion care should consider the values and preferences of the individual seeking care, available resources, and the national and local context. A plurality of service delivery approaches can coexist within any given context. 13. It is essential to ensure that individuals seeking abortion care have access to scientifically accurate and understandable information, quality medications (including those for pain management), backup referral support if needed, and appropriate contraceptive services for those desiring post-abortion contraception. 14. The evidence supporting community-based outreach models, harm-reduction counseling, and self-sourcing of medications for abortion care is insufficient to formulate strong recommendations. However, good practice statements should address the range of counseling and support models available in the context of medical abortion care.
